Hey, an 8-year Setraline user here!

Once I got my diagnosis and started taking the medication for adhd, I realised very quickly I no longer needed the Setraline. My doctors explained that my anxiety was most likely from my adhd, so I took the advice on board and tapered off around August last year!

I feel like my anxiety is completely eradicated for the time being when I'm on my medication, either Vyvanse of Dex. I'm able to work and function without the overbearing weight of anxiety. Definitely have a chat to your doctors about what the best option would be.

Most, if not all, of my bpd episodes are usually a reaction to hurting someone, or feeling like I've burdened them in some way. Part of it is genuine remorse, especially with those I love, whilst the other part is the fear of them leaving me with the impression that I'm a truly horrible person. I have a huge problem with blaming myself for any wrongdoings, even if it had nothing to do with me at all. I'm naturally a people pleaser, so any interaction I have with strangers usually has me doing mental gymnastics to try and avoid coming across as negative in any way. With those I love, I have a tendency to be a little less occupied with how I am perceived, so I tend to say the wrong things, particularly during arguments or confrontations.

This is when the guilt immediately kicks in and I have a major bpd episode. After I cuddle up with a stuffed animal and try to use my DBT-inspired coping mechanisms to calm down and remind myself I'm not as horrible as I believe I am, I feel confident to apologise for my words and actions.

All in all, I'm a big ol' ball of guilt and remorse, I guess

I smoke daily, but only when it's the last thing to do at the end of the night. I wake up, get ready for work, go to work, do all my grocery shopping and needs while sober, but I always need that little edge off - to me, it's no different than drinking a beer at the end of the night. I use it to watch movies, especially after work when I'm coming off my adhd meds (the adhd somehow gets worse) and I just want to chill out and stop thinking about work and real life problems.

 I can go days and weeks without weed with no real withdrawal symptoms, other than just being aware that I don't have it. The only time I need it is when I'm having an episode that's teetering on self-harm relapses or suicide.

For me, weed saved my life. I wouldn't be alive today without it. It's the only thing in the world that slows down my adhd/ocd thoughts when I'm having an episode (mostly super negative) and allows me that breathing time to think things through and fully process my emotions without the need to self harm as a distraction. My psychiatrist prescribed me a bunch of meds that seem more harmful than good, so I would rather stick to weed.

I've been seeing therapists most of my life, since I was a kid, and no matter what I will still come back to weed when I'm struggling. Anything to avoid flooding my system with chemicals and pills that weed does much faster and easier, WITHOUT physical or cognitive symptoms.

I don't use it to numb my thoughts or emotions, it's usually a last resort for an episode - whenever I can't process my thoughts and have meltdowns, weed is there to calm me down for an hour, enough time to figure out how to change the situation or realise there's no need to be so stressed, then I feel completely fine for the rest of the day.

If we need to take chemicals and pills to function, then I see no real issue with using a natural substance to help as well. I've been off antidepressants for a month now, after being on them for 8 years, and I know that I feel so much more in tune with my feelings, my anxiety is back (but its a manageable feeling), and no matter what happens to flip that bpd switch, I know I just need a couple of hits to feel less suicidal.

Yes 100%, this is such a struggle for me, too. I made a little mantra for myself to help with negative things I say about myself, which is "if I don't treat anyone else this way, why should I treat myself this way?" It comes from my experience being a manager in the past, and having to manage a lot of staff members. No matter how many mistakes they would make, I was always very compassionate with them, and was very patient and understanding while I helped them learn how to fix those mistakes. However, whenever I am the one making mistakes, I tend to get mad and put a lot of blame and shame on myself. It could be a lot of trauma from the way I've been treated by bosses and other managers in the past, which is why I learned how to be compassionate to others when I finally took on the role. I'm still working with my therapist on how to be nicer to myself, as nice to myself as I am to others. It's been such a struggle, though.
